claims.claim: A loan is money borrowed that is repaid over time, usually with interest; the SEC's Investor.gov glossary describes debt as an amount owed for borrowed funds that is normally repaid with interest on a schedule set out in the repayment terms.
The principal of a loan is the amount of money borrowed, on which interest is calculated.
Interest is the price paid for borrowing money, quoted as a percentage per period.
Loans have a repayment period (the term); the longer repayment takes, the more interest the borrower pays, because interest is charged for more time.

Installment loans are closed-end loans: the lender gives the borrower all of the money at the beginning, and the borrower repays it in set, fixed amounts over a specific period, with the payment generally the same throughout the loan.

A secured loan is backed by collateral — an asset the borrower pledges that the lender can take if the loan is not repaid; an unsecured loan has no collateral, so the lender relies on the borrower's creditworthiness.

Revolving credit is an open-end arrangement: the borrower has a credit limit, receives a monthly bill, makes at least a minimum payment, pays interest on the outstanding balance, and can borrow again as the balance is paid down.

The overall cost of a loan is interest plus any fees — common categories include origination fees, documentation fees, credit insurance, and late fees; the APR expresses the total cost, including interest charges and fees, as a yearly rate.

What to compare across loans, stated factually: the annual percentage rate (and whether and how much it can change), the term, and the fees (access, annual, late); sources note it pays to shop around and compare offers from multiple lenders.
Honest framing: borrowing is a way to purchase something now and pay for it over time, so a loan trades future income for present needs; the lesson states this without advice.

conflictingEvidence: Definition wording varies across sources: MyMoney.gov describes borrowing as purchasing now and paying over time, CFI defines a loan as a sum of money paid back with interest within a given period, and Investor.gov defines debt as borrowed funds typically repaid with interest by a specific date. The lesson uses the working definition 'money borrowed that is repaid over time, usually with interest' and attributes the idea to these sources.

Example loans used to illustrate secured versus unsecured differ by source (CFI lists credit-card purchases among unsecured borrowings; CFPB treats credit cards as revolving accounts). The lesson keeps the classification general, uses original examples, and leaves credit-card mechanics to the sibling credit-cards topic.

Fee names and amounts vary by lender and loan type; CFPB lists common categories (origination, documentation, credit insurance, late fees) without universal amounts. The lesson names categories and avoids quoting any fee as universal.

The machine-generated draft called loans 'a foundational concept' used as a 'building block' for later discussion — boilerplate with no evidential support; it was replaced entirely by the source-verified working definition and mechanics.
unsupportedExistingClaims: Draft's framing of loans as 'a foundational concept in Personal Finance' introduced as a 'building block for later discussions' — boilerplate, not supported by any source.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the boilerplate definition with the attributed working definition (borrowed money repaid over time, usually with interest).

sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live via curl on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: personal installment loans as closed-end loans where the lender gives all the money at the beginning and the borrower repays in set or fixed amounts over a specific period; payments generally the same throughout the loan; loan sizes and lengths ranging from a few months to several years. sourceRecords.title: Do personal installment loans have fees? (CFPB Ask CFPB)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live via curl on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: installment loans repaid in periodic fixed amounts; fees (origination, documentation, credit insurance generally optional, late fees) factor into the overall cost of the loan along with the interest paid to the lender; the advice-neutral fact that borrowers should shop around and compare offers between multiple lenders. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: What is a personal line of credit? (CFPB Ask CFPB)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live via curl on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: like a credit-card account, a line of credit has a credit limit, a monthly bill, at least a minimum payment, interest based on the outstanding balance, and possibly a fee per use; personal lines of credit are unsecured, while home equity lines of credit (HELOCs) are backed by a mortgage on the home. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: What should I look for when shopping for a personal line of credit? (CFPB Ask CFPB)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live via curl on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports, stated factually: look at the annual percentage rate (APR), whether and how much the APR can change, and fees — fees to access the line, annual fees, late payment fees, and fees for other events — and compare the costs with other types of credit. No recommendations made by the lesson. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.
